front: Give the order air passes through on the way to the alveoli.
back: **Trachea ➔ bronchus ➔ bronchiole ➔ alveolus**

front: What is the function of the ribs?
back: A **bone structure** that **protects the internal organs**, such as the lungs.

front: What is the function of the intercostal muscles?
back: They lie **between the ribs** and **control their movement**, causing inhalation and exhalation.

front: What is the function of the diaphragm?
back: A sheet of **connective tissue and muscle** at the bottom of the thorax that helps **change the volume of the thorax** to allow inhalation and exhalation.

front: What is the function of the trachea?
back: The **windpipe**, which connects the mouth and nose to the lungs.

front: What are the bronchi?
back:
The **large tubes** branching off the trachea that connect to the bronchioles.

Human lungs contain **two** — one **bronchus** each.

front: What are the bronchioles?
back: The **smaller tubes** that connect the bronchi to the alveoli.

front: What are the alveoli?
back:
Tiny, **balloon-like air sacs** at the ends of the bronchioles.

They are the **specialised gas exchange surfaces**, where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

front: What are the pleural membranes?
back: **Thin layers of tissue** that surround the lungs and line the inside of the thorax.

front: Name four adaptations of the human respiratory system.
back:
- A **large surface area**, provided by many alveoli
- Alveolus and capillary walls that are **one cell thick**
- **Good ventilation** with air
- A **good blood supply**

The last three all help **maintain a high concentration gradient**.

front: The windpipe that connects the mouth and nose to the lungs is the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: The windpipe that connects the mouth and nose to the lungs is the **trachea**.

front: Gas exchange takes place in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ at the ends of the bronchioles.
back: Gas exchange takes place in the **alveoli** at the ends of the bronchioles.

front:
**True or False?**

Air passes through the bronchioles before the bronchi.
back:
**False.**

Air passes through the **trachea**, then the **bronchi**, and only then the **bronchioles**.

front:
**True or False?**

A good blood supply maintains a high concentration gradient.
back:
**True.**

It carries blood with a **high concentration of oxygen away** from the alveoli, keeping the gradient steep for diffusion.

front: Why are there two sets of intercostal muscles?
back:
Because muscles can only **pull** on bones, never push.

The **external** and **internal** intercostal muscles therefore work **antagonistically**.

front: What do the external intercostal muscles do?
back: They **contract to pull the rib cage up** during **inhalation**.

front: What do the internal intercostal muscles do?
back: They **contract to pull the rib cage down** during **forced exhalation**.

front: Where is the diaphragm and what is it?
back: A **thin sheet of muscle** that **separates the chest cavity from the abdomen**.

front: Describe what happens during inhalation.
back:
The **diaphragm contracts** and flattens.

The **external intercostal muscles contract**, pulling the ribs **up and out**.

The **volume** of the thorax **increases**, so the **air pressure** inside the lungs **decreases** relative to outside.

Air is **drawn in**.

front: Describe what happens during normal exhalation.
back:
The **diaphragm relaxes** and moves upwards into its domed shape.

The **external intercostal muscles relax**, so the ribs **drop down and inwards**.

The **volume** of the thorax **decreases**, so the **air pressure** inside the lungs **increases** relative to outside.

Air is **forced out**.

front: What is forced exhalation?
back: When the **internal** intercostal muscles also contract to pull the ribs **down and in**, decreasing the thorax volume further and forcing air out **more quickly**.

front: When is forced exhalation needed, and why?
back:
During **strenuous activity**, when there is a greater need to remove the **increased carbon dioxide** produced.

It allows a **greater volume of gases to be exchanged**.

front: What happens to the pressure in the lungs as their volume increases?
back: The pressure **decreases** relative to outside the body, so air is **drawn in**.

front: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and **flattens**.

front: During normal exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and returns to its ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ shape.
back: During normal exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and returns to its **domed** shape.

front:
**True or False?**

The internal intercostal muscles are used during normal exhalation.
back:
**False.**

Normal exhalation only needs the **external** intercostal muscles to **relax**. The internal ones contract during **forced** exhalation.

front:
**True or False?**

Inspiration and inhalation mean the same thing.
back:
**True.**

**Inhalation / inspiration** both mean breathing in, and **exhalation / expiration** both mean breathing out.

front: Name five adaptations of the alveoli for gas exchange.
back:
- Many rounded **alveolar sacs**, giving a very large **surface area to volume ratio**
- **Thin, single layers of cells** in the alveoli and capillaries
- **Ventilation**, maintaining a steep concentration gradient
- A **good blood supply**
- A **layer of moisture** on the alveolar surface

front: Why do the many rounded alveolar sacs help gas exchange?
back: They give a very **large surface area to volume ratio**, so more gas can diffuse at the same time.

front: Why are the walls of the alveoli and capillaries so thin?
back: They are **single layers of cells**, which **minimises the diffusion distance** for the gases.

front: How does ventilation maintain a steep concentration gradient?
back: It keeps **oxygen levels high** and **carbon dioxide levels low** in the alveolar air space.

front: How does a good blood supply maintain the concentration gradient?
back: It ensures a constant supply of blood that is **high in carbon dioxide** and **low in oxygen**, keeping the gradient steep in both directions.

front: Why is the layer of moisture on the alveoli important?
back: The gases can **dissolve** in it, which helps them **diffuse**.

front: In which direction does each gas diffuse at an alveolus?
back:
- **Oxygen** diffuses **from the alveolar air into the blood**
- **Carbon dioxide** diffuses **from the blood into the alveolar air**

front: The walls of the alveoli and their capillaries are only ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ cell thick.
back: The walls of the alveoli and their capillaries are only **one** cell thick.

front: A layer of ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ on the alveolar surface lets the gases dissolve.
back: A layer of **moisture** on the alveolar surface lets the gases dissolve.

front:
**True or False?**

Blood arriving at the alveoli is high in oxygen.
back:
**False.**

Blood arriving at the alveoli is **low in oxygen** and **high in carbon dioxide** — which is what maintains the concentration gradients for diffusion.

front:
**True or False?**

Gas exchange at the alveoli happens by diffusion.
back:
**True.**

Every alveolar adaptation exists to make **diffusion** between the air in the lungs and the blood in the capillaries as fast as possible.

front: Why does a large surface area speed up gas exchange?
back: More **particles can diffuse across the surface at the same time**, so the overall rate of exchange is higher.

front: How does nicotine affect the circulatory system?
back:
It **narrows blood vessels** and **increases heart rate**, raising **blood pressure**.

High blood pressure can cause **blood clots** in the arteries, leading to a **heart attack** or **stroke**.

front: How does carbon monoxide reduce oxygen transport?
back: It **binds irreversibly to haemoglobin**, reducing the **oxygen-carrying capacity** of the blood.

front: Why does carbon monoxide strain the breathing system?
back: **Breathing frequency and depth must increase** to supply the same amount of oxygen, because less can be carried by the blood.

front: How does carbon monoxide increase the risk of heart disease?
back: The circulatory system must **pump blood faster**, which **raises blood pressure** and increases the risk of **coronary heart disease** and **stroke**.

front: Why is tar in cigarettes dangerous?
back:
Tar is a **carcinogen**, linked to an increased chance of **cancerous cells** developing in the lungs.

It also contributes to **COPD**.

front: Define **carcinogen**.
back: A substance, such as the **tar** in cigarettes, that increases the chance of **cancerous cells** developing.

front: Which two conditions occurring together make up COPD?
back:
- **Chronic bronchitis**
- **Emphysema**

front: How does tar cause chronic bronchitis?
back:
It stimulates **goblet cells and mucus glands** to enlarge and **produce more mucus**.

Mucus **builds up**, blocking the smallest **bronchioles** and leading to infections.

front: Why can smokers not clear the mucus from their airways?
back:
The build-up of mucus **damages the cilia**, so they cannot **beat** to move mucus up and out of the lungs.

A **smoker's cough** is the attempt to move it instead.

front: How does emphysema develop?
back:
Repeated **infections and inflammation** damage the walls of the alveoli, so many of them **break down and burst**.

This **reduces the surface area** available for gas exchange.

front: What are the symptoms of emphysema?
back: Patients become **breathless and wheezy**, and may need a **constant supply of oxygen** to stay alive.

front: Why do smokers get lung infections more often?
back: Because of the **build-up of mucus** in the lungs, which the damaged cilia cannot remove.

front: Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly to ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
back: Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly to **haemoglobin**, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

front: Tar damages the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ lining the airways, so mucus can no longer be swept out of the lungs.
back: Tar damages the **cilia** lining the airways, so mucus can no longer be swept out of the lungs.

front:
**True or False?**

Emphysema increases the surface area available for gas exchange.
back:
**False.**

The alveoli burst, which **reduces** the surface area for gas exchange.

front:
**True or False?**

Smoking is a risk factor for coronary heart disease.
back:
**True.**

Both **nicotine** and **carbon monoxide** raise blood pressure, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.

front: Outline the method for investigating exercise and breathing rate.
back:
Each participant **sits quietly for 1 minute** and counts their breaths.

Each then performs the **same exercise**, such as running on the spot for 1 minute.

**Immediately after** exercise, count the breaths taken in 1 minute again.

Calculate the **change in breathing rate**, then repeat and find **mean values**.

front: What counts as one breath when measuring breathing rate?
back: **One inhale plus one exhale**.

front: How is the change in breathing rate calculated?
back: **breathing rate after exercise − breathing rate at rest**

front: What effect does exercise have on breathing?
back: It increases both the **frequency** and the **depth** of breathing.

front: Why is an increased breathing rate useful during exercise?
back: It allows **more oxygen to be taken in** and **carbon dioxide to be removed more quickly**.

front: Which variables should be kept the same in this investigation?
back:
- **Type and duration** of exercise
- **Environment**, including temperature
- **Rest period** before measuring
- **Time of day**
- **Method of counting** breaths

front: Why is varying exercise intensity a limitation?
back:
Participants may **work harder or less hard** depending on motivation or ability.

Using a **controlled exercise**, such as step-ups at a set pace or cycling at a fixed power output, improves consistency.

front: Why is breathing rate difficult to measure accurately?
back:
It **changes quickly after exercise**, and timing or counting errors reduce reliability.

An improvement is to start counting **immediately** and measure a **short fixed period**, such as 15 seconds, then multiply up.

front: Which external conditions can affect breathing rate?
back:
**Temperature**, **air quality** and **stress levels**.

Running the investigation **indoors** in similar conditions for everyone reduces their effect.

front: Why is it hard to control variables between participants?
back: Their **fitness**, **lifestyle** and any **health conditions** all differ and cannot easily be matched.

front: Exercise increases both the frequency and the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ of breathing.
back: Exercise increases both the frequency and the **depth** of breathing.

front: Repeating the measurement with several participants allows a ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ to be calculated.
back: Repeating the measurement with several participants allows a **mean** to be calculated.

front:
**True or False?**

Breathing rate should be measured immediately after exercise ends.
back:
**True.**

Breathing rate **falls quickly** once exercise stops, so any delay would underestimate the effect.

front:
**True or False?**

A single participant is enough for a reliable conclusion.
back:
**False.**

**Several participants** are needed so that a **mean** can be calculated and individual differences do not distort the result.

front: By which three processes do cells exchange substances?
back:
- **Diffusion**
- **Osmosis**
- **Active transport**

All across the **cell membrane**.

front: Why can unicellular organisms rely on diffusion alone?
back:
They have a **large surface area relative to their volume**, so the distance from the surface to the centre is **small**.

Diffusion, osmosis and active transport through the cell membrane are therefore **sufficient**.

front: Give an example of a unicellular organism with no transport system.
back: An **amoeba**.

front: Why do multicellular organisms need a transport system?
back:
They have **multiple cell layers**, so the distance from the surface to the centre is **too long** for diffusion alone.

Diffusion to every cell would be **too slow** to meet the organism's needs.

front: Which transport system do animals have, and what does it carry?
back: The **circulatory system**, which carries substances in the **blood** — for example oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide, water and urea.

front: Which transport system do plants have?
back:
The **vascular system**:

- **Xylem** — moves water and mineral ions from roots to shoots
- **Phloem** — distributes sugars and amino acids through the plant

front: Unicellular organisms have a large ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ relative to their volume, so diffusion is sufficient.
back: Unicellular organisms have a large **surface area** relative to their volume, so diffusion is sufficient.

front: In animals, substances are carried around the body by the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ system.
back: In animals, substances are carried around the body by the **circulatory** system.

front:
**True or False?**

An amoeba needs a specialised exchange surface.
back:
**False.**

Its **surface area to volume ratio** is large enough that the cell membrane alone can meet its exchange needs.

front:
**True or False?**

Diffusion alone would be too slow to supply every cell in a human.
back:
**True.**

This is exactly why larger, multicellular organisms need a **transport system**.

front: Why must all organisms exchange substances with their environment?
back: To take in **food molecules** and remove **waste**, so that they can function properly.

front: Name four substances carried in human blood.
back:
- **Oxygen**
- **Glucose**
- **Carbon dioxide**
- **Urea**

**Water** is also transported.

front: What does the xylem transport, and in which direction?
back: **Water** and **mineral ions**, from the **roots** to other parts of the plant.

front: What does the phloem transport?
back: **Sucrose** and **amino acids**, from where they are produced or stored to where they are needed.

front: Describe the structure of a xylem vessel.
back:
A **hollow tube of dead cells** with the end walls broken down, reinforced by **lignin**.

This gives an unbroken channel for **water** to travel from the roots to the rest of the plant.

front: Describe the structure of the phloem.
back: A tube formed from **living cells**, with **small holes** through which substances can move.

front: Why does the phloem carry sucrose away from the leaves?
back: Because sucrose and amino acids are **produced in the leaves** during photosynthesis, and must be moved to other parts of the plant that need them.

front: Which two tissues make up the transport system of a plant?
back:
- **Xylem**
- **Phloem**

front: Xylem vessels are reinforced by ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, which strengthens the hollow tube.
back: Xylem vessels are reinforced by **lignin**, which strengthens the hollow tube.

front: The phloem transports ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ and amino acids around the plant.
back: The phloem transports **sucrose** and amino acids around the plant.

front:
**True or False?**

Xylem vessels are made of living cells.
back:
**False.**

Xylem is a hollow tube of **dead cells** reinforced by lignin. It is the **phloem** that is made of living cells.

front:
**True or False?**

The xylem carries water only upwards from the roots.
back:
**True.**

Water and mineral ions travel in one direction only — **from the roots to other parts of the plant**.

front: Why does a multicellular plant need a transport system?
back: Most of its cells are **too far from the surface** for diffusion alone to supply them quickly enough, because it has a **small surface area to volume ratio**.

front: Give one structural difference between xylem and phloem.
back: Xylem is made of **dead cells** with the walls between them broken down; phloem is made of **living cells** with small holes between them.

front: Name the four components of blood.
back:
- **Red blood cells**
- **White blood cells**
- **Platelets**
- **Plasma**

front: Which component makes up over half the volume of blood?
back:
**Plasma**.

Most of the other half is **red blood cells**, with white blood cells and platelets making up the small remaining fraction.

front: Describe the structure of a red blood cell.
back: A **biconcave disc** with **no nucleus**, containing **haemoglobin**.

front: Describe the structure of a white blood cell.
back:
A **large cell** containing a **large nucleus**.

Different types have slightly different structures and functions.

front: What are platelets?
back: **Fragments of cells**.

front: Describe the appearance of plasma.
back: A **clear, straw-coloured aqueous solution**, in which the other blood components are suspended.

front: Name five things plasma transports.
back:
- **Carbon dioxide**, from respiring cells to the lungs
- **Digested food and mineral ions**, from the small intestine to cells
- **Urea**, to the kidneys
- **Hormones**, from glands to target organs
- **Heat energy**, to cooler parts of the body or to the skin

front: Where does plasma carry carbon dioxide from and to?
back: **From respiring cells to the lungs**, dissolved in the plasma.

front: Where does plasma transport urea to?
back: The **kidneys**.

front: Give the three adaptations of red blood cells for carrying oxygen.
back:
- Packed with **haemoglobin**, a protein that binds oxygen to form **oxyhaemoglobin**
- **No nucleus**, leaving more space for haemoglobin
- A **biconcave disc shape**, giving a larger **surface area to volume ratio** for fast diffusion

front: What does haemoglobin form when it binds to oxygen?
back: **Oxyhaemoglobin**.

front: Why is the biconcave disc shape useful?
back: It makes the cell **thinner in the middle than at the edges**, giving a **larger surface area to volume ratio** so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.

front: Red blood cells have no ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, which leaves more room for haemoglobin.
back: Red blood cells have no **nucleus**, which leaves more room for haemoglobin.

front: Hormones are chemical messengers transported around the body in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Hormones are chemical messengers transported around the body in the **plasma**.

front:
**True or False?**

Plasma helps distribute heat around the body.
back:
**True.**

Heat energy created in **respiration** is transferred in the plasma to **cooler parts** of the body, or to the **skin** where it can be lost.

front:
**True or False?**

Platelets are complete cells.
back:
**False.**

Platelets are **fragments of cells**.

front: Name the two main types of white blood cell.
back:
- **Phagocytes**
- **Lymphocytes**

front: How does a phagocyte destroy a pathogen?
back:
Its **sensitive cell surface membrane** detects chemicals produced by the pathogen.

It then **engulfs** the pathogen and releases **digestive enzymes** to digest it.

front: Why is phagocytosis described as a non-specific response?
back: Because a phagocyte will engulf and digest **any** pathogen it encounters, not just one particular type.

front: Define **antigen**.
back: A **marker on the surface of a cell or pathogen** that the body recognises as **foreign**, causing the immune system to respond.

front: Define **antibody**.
back:
A **protein** made by **lymphocytes** whose shape is **complementary to an antigen**.

When attached, it clumps pathogens together and marks them for destruction.

front: Why is the lymphocyte response described as specific?
back: Because the antibodies produced will only **fit one type of antigen**.

front: Describe the immune response to an infection.
back:
The pathogen enters the bloodstream and **multiplies**, releasing **toxins** and infecting body cells, which causes **symptoms**.

**Phagocytes** engulf and digest pathogens they encounter.

**Lymphocytes** recognise the pathogen and release **antibodies specific to it**.

Antibodies **bind to the pathogens** and mark them for destruction, and **phagocytes** engulf them.

front: How does a white blood cell differ from a red blood cell?
back:
- A white blood cell **has a nucleus**; a red blood cell does not
- White blood cells **defend against pathogens**; red blood cells **transport oxygen**

front: Why can a pathogen still make you ill before the immune response works?
back:
**Lymphocytes** take time to produce enough **specific antibodies**.

In the meantime the pathogen **multiplies** and releases **toxins**, causing symptoms.

front: How do the roles of phagocytes and lymphocytes differ?
back:
- **Phagocytes** **engulf and digest** pathogens — this works against **any** pathogen
- **Lymphocytes** release **antibodies** that are **specific** to one pathogen

front: What is the role of the immune system once a pathogen enters?
back: To **prevent the infectious organism from reproducing** and to **destroy** it.

front: Antibodies are produced by ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, a type of white blood cell.
back: Antibodies are produced by **lymphocytes**, a type of white blood cell.

front: Phagocytes engulf pathogens and release digestive ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ to break them down.
back: Phagocytes engulf pathogens and release digestive **enzymes** to break them down.

front:
**True or False?**

One antibody can bind to any antigen.
back:
**False.**

Each antibody's shape is **complementary to one specific antigen**, so it fits only that one.

front:
**True or False?**

Antibodies destroy pathogens by digesting them.
back:
**False.**

Antibodies **bind to the pathogen** and mark it for destruction — the digesting is done by **phagocytes**.

front: Why is the heart described as a double pump?
back:
The **left** side pumps **oxygenated** blood from the lungs to the rest of the body (the **systemic circuit**).

The **right** side pumps **deoxygenated** blood from the body to the lungs (the **pulmonary circuit**).

front: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
back: Because it must pump blood at **high pressure around the entire body**, while the right ventricle only pumps at **lower pressure to the lungs**.

front: Define **septum**.
back: The **muscle wall** that **separates the two sides** of the heart.

front: What is the function of the coronary arteries?
back: They supply the heart's own **cardiac muscle tissue** with **oxygenated blood**, so it can respire aerobically and keep contracting.

front: What is the function of the valves in the heart?
back: To **prevent blood flowing backwards**.

front: Trace deoxygenated blood from the body to the lungs.
back:
It flows through the **vena cava** into the **right atrium**.

The atrium contracts, forcing blood through the **tricuspid valve** into the **right ventricle**.

The ventricle contracts, pushing blood through the **semilunar valve** into the **pulmonary artery**, and on to the lungs.

front: Trace oxygenated blood from the lungs to the body.
back:
It returns via the **pulmonary vein** into the **left atrium**.

The atrium contracts, forcing blood through the **bicuspid valve** into the **left ventricle**.

The ventricle contracts, pushing blood through the **semilunar valve** and out of the **aorta**.

front: Why is blood pumped to the lungs at low pressure?
back: To **prevent damage** to the delicate **capillaries** in the lungs.

front: In which direction do arteries and veins carry blood?
back:
- **Arteries** carry blood **away** from the heart
- **Veins** carry blood **towards** the heart

front: Which valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle?
back: The **bicuspid** (atrioventricular) valve.

front: Which valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle?
back: The **tricuspid** (atrioventricular) valve.

front: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the heart through the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the heart through the **vena cava**.

front: Oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the **aorta**.

front:
**True or False?**

Both atria contract at the same time.
back:
**True.**

Both **atria** contract together, and both **ventricles** contract together — even though the pathway is usually described one chamber at a time.

front:
**True or False?**

The left side of a heart diagram shows the heart's left side.
back:
**False.**

The heart is **labelled as if it were in the chest**, so the **left** of the diagram is the patient's **right** side, and vice versa.

front: How is heart rate measured?
back: By counting the number of times the heart **beats in a minute** (bpm).

front: Define **adrenaline**.
back: A **hormone** released by the **adrenal glands** that prepares the body for action.

front: Where is adrenaline produced?
back: In the **adrenal glands**, which sit just above the **kidneys**.

front: Why does the heart rate increase during exercise?
back: Muscle cells **respire faster** to release more energy for contraction, increasing the demand for **oxygen and glucose** and for the **removal of carbon dioxide**.

front: What two changes does the nervous system make during exercise?
back:
- **Increases heart rate**, so oxygen and glucose arrive faster and carbon dioxide is removed faster
- **Increases the volume of blood** pumped per beat, so more blood reaches the muscles each minute

front: Why does the heart rate stay high after exercise ends?
back: To keep supplying the **oxygen** needed to break down the **lactic acid** that built up during anaerobic respiration.

front: How does adrenaline affect the heart rate?
back: It **increases** heart rate as part of the **'fight or flight'** response, preparing the body for action.

front: Why does the heart pump blood to respiring cells?
back: To **supply oxygen and glucose** for respiration and to **remove carbon dioxide**.

front: When does anaerobic respiration occur during exercise?
back:
During **intense exercise**, when the **oxygen supply is insufficient** to meet the muscle cells' energy needs.

Aerobic respiration still continues at the same time.

front: During exercise the heart rate ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, so oxygen reaches the muscles faster.
back: During exercise the heart rate **increases**, so oxygen reaches the muscles faster.

front: The hormone ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ increases heart rate as part of the fight or flight response.
back: The hormone **adrenaline** increases heart rate as part of the fight or flight response.

front:
**True or False?**

Heart rate returns to normal the moment exercise stops.
back:
**False.**

It **remains high** for a period, to supply the oxygen needed to break down the **lactic acid** built up during anaerobic respiration.

front:
**True or False?**

Exercise increases the volume of blood pumped per heartbeat.
back:
**True.**

Both the **rate** and the **volume per beat** increase, so much more blood reaches the muscles each minute.

front: What happens to the coronary arteries in coronary heart disease?
back: Layers of **fatty material (plaque)** build up inside them, **narrowing the lumen** and reducing blood flow to the cardiac muscle.

front: What are the fatty deposits in the coronary arteries mainly made of?
back: **Cholesterol**.

front: What are the two sources of cholesterol in the body?
back:
- **Dietary cholesterol**, from animal products eaten
- Cholesterol **synthesised by the liver**

front: What does a partial blockage of a coronary artery cause?
back: **Restricted blood flow** to the cardiac muscle cells, causing severe chest pains called **angina**.

front: What does a complete blockage of a coronary artery cause?
back: A **heart attack** — cells in that area of the heart can no longer respire **aerobically**.

front: Name four risk factors for coronary heart disease.
back:
- **Obesity**
- **High blood pressure**
- **High cholesterol**
- **Smoking**

front: Why does obesity increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
back: Carrying extra weight **puts a strain on the heart**, and can lead to **Type 2 diabetes**, which further damages the blood vessels.

front: Why does high blood pressure increase the risk?
back: It increases the **force of the blood against the artery walls**, which **damages the vessels**.

front: Why does high cholesterol increase the risk?
back: It **speeds up the build-up of fatty plaques** in the arteries, leading to blockages.

front: Give three ways smoking increases the risk of heart disease.
back:
- Chemicals in smoke increase **plaque build-up**
- They also increase **blood pressure**
- **Carbon monoxide** reduces the **oxygen-carrying capacity** of red blood cells

front: What do the coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with?
back: **Oxygen** and **glucose**.

front: The fatty plaques that build up in the coronary arteries are formed mainly from ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: The fatty plaques that build up in the coronary arteries are formed mainly from **cholesterol**.

front: Severe chest pain caused by restricted blood flow to the heart muscle is called ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Severe chest pain caused by restricted blood flow to the heart muscle is called **angina**.

front:
**True or False?**

All the cholesterol in the body comes from the diet.
back:
**False.**

Some is **dietary**, from animal products, but cholesterol is also **synthesised by the liver**.

front:
**True or False?**

Obesity can lead to Type 2 diabetes, which damages blood vessels.
back:
**True.**

This is one of the ways obesity raises the risk of coronary heart disease, alongside the extra strain on the heart.

front: Name the three main types of blood vessel.
back:
- **Arteries**
- **Veins**
- **Capillaries**

front: What are arterioles and venules?
back:
- **Arterioles** — the smaller vessels that branch off arteries
- **Venules** — the small vessels that join to form veins

front: Give the key features of an artery.
back:
- Carries blood at **high pressure away from the heart**
- Carries **oxygenated** blood, except the pulmonary artery
- **Thick muscular walls** containing **elastic fibres**
- A **narrow lumen**
- Blood flows **fast**

front: How is an artery adapted to its function?
back:
The **thick muscular walls with elastic fibres** withstand the high pressure and **maintain** it by **recoiling** after blood has passed.

The **narrow lumen** also helps maintain the high pressure.

front: Give the key features of a vein.
back:
- Carries blood at **low pressure towards the heart**
- Carries **deoxygenated** blood, except the pulmonary vein
- **Thin walls** and a **large lumen**
- Contains **valves**
- Blood flows **slowly**

front: How is a vein adapted to its function?
back:
Its **large lumen reduces resistance** to blood flowing under low pressure.

Its **valves prevent the backflow** of blood.

front: Give the key features of a capillary.
back:
- Carries blood at **low pressure** within tissues
- Carries **both oxygenated and deoxygenated** blood
- Walls are **one cell thick** and **'leaky'**
- Blood flows **slowly**

front: How is a capillary adapted to its function?
back:
Walls **one cell thick** give a **short diffusion distance**, so substances diffuse in and out easily.

**'Leaky' walls** let blood plasma leak out and form **tissue fluid** around the cells.

front: Why do veins need valves but arteries do not?
back: Blood in veins is under **low pressure**, so it could **flow backwards**. Blood in arteries is under **high pressure**, which keeps it moving forwards.

front: Arteries have a narrow lumen and thick muscular walls to withstand ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ blood pressure.
back: Arteries have a narrow lumen and thick muscular walls to withstand **high** blood pressure.

front: Plasma leaking out of capillaries forms ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, which surrounds the cells.
back: Plasma leaking out of capillaries forms **tissue fluid**, which surrounds the cells.

front:
**True or False?**

All arteries carry oxygenated blood.
back:
**False.**

The **pulmonary artery** is the exception — it carries **deoxygenated** blood from the heart to the lungs.

front:
**True or False?**

Capillary walls are one cell thick.
back:
**True.**

This gives a **short diffusion distance**, so substances can pass in and out easily.

front: Which vessel carries blood most slowly, and why does that help?
back: The **capillaries**. Slow flow at **low pressure** gives more **time for diffusion** of substances into and out of the surrounding tissues.

front: Describe the general structure of the circulatory system.
back: A **closed network** of blood vessels connected to the **heart**, with blood flowing in **one direction**.

front: Trace the vessels from an artery to a vein within an organ.
back:
**Artery ➔ arteriole ➔ capillary ➔ venule ➔ vein**

Respiring cells in the organ use up the oxygen from the blood in the capillaries.

front: Which artery and vein are exceptions to the usual rule?
back:
- The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood away from the heart
- The **pulmonary vein** carries **oxygenated** blood to the heart

front: Name the vessels carrying blood to and from the heart.
back:
- **Towards** — vena cava and pulmonary vein
- **Away** — aorta and pulmonary artery

front: Name the vessels carrying blood to and from the lungs.
back:
- **Towards** — pulmonary artery
- **Away** — pulmonary vein

front: Name the vessels carrying blood to and from the liver.
back:
- **Towards** — hepatic artery **and** hepatic portal vein
- **Away** — hepatic vein

front: Name the vessels carrying blood to and from the kidneys.
back:
- **Towards** — renal artery
- **Away** — renal vein

front: Why does the liver receive blood from two vessels?
back:
- The **hepatic artery** brings **oxygenated** blood
- The **hepatic portal vein** brings blood carrying the **products of digestion** from the small intestine

front: Why does blood leaving an organ usually carry less oxygen?
back: Because the **respiring cells** in the organ have **used up the oxygen** from the blood.

front: The liver is unusual because it receives blood from both the hepatic artery and the hepatic ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ vein.
back: The liver is unusual because it receives blood from both the hepatic artery and the hepatic **portal** vein.

front: Blood is carried away from the kidney in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ vein.
back: Blood is carried away from the kidney in the **renal** vein.

front:
**True or False?**

Blood in the circulatory system can flow in either direction.
back:
**False.**

The circulatory system is a **closed network** in which blood flows in **one direction** only.

front:
**True or False?**

The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.
back:
**True.**

It is the exception among veins, carrying **oxygenated** blood from the lungs back to the heart.

front: Which two waste gases must leave a plant?
back:
- **Oxygen**
- **Carbon dioxide**

Each can be **both a reactant and a waste product**, depending on the time of day.

front: Which gas is in excess during the day, and why?
back:
**Oxygen**.

The rate of **photosynthesis is higher** than the rate of respiration, so **more oxygen is produced than used**.

front: Which gas is in excess at night, and why?
back:
**Carbon dioxide**.

There is **no photosynthesis, only respiration**, so carbon dioxide is produced and none is used up.

front: Through which structures do waste gases leave a plant?
back: The **stomata**, in the **leaf**.

front: Why is excretion in plants not technically an active process?
back: Because the excess gases leave by **diffusion**, which requires **no energy** from the plant.

front: What happens to plant waste products that are not excreted?
back: Some are **used up in other processes** within the plant.

front: Which organ is responsible for excretion in a plant?
back: The **leaf**.

front: Waste gases diffuse out of a plant through the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ in the leaf.
back: Waste gases diffuse out of a plant through the **stomata** in the leaf.

front: During the day a plant excretes excess ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, the waste product of photosynthesis.
back: During the day a plant excretes excess **oxygen**, the waste product of photosynthesis.

front:
**True or False?**

Photosynthesis stops at night but respiration continues.
back:
**True.**

With insufficient light there is **no photosynthesis, only respiration**, so carbon dioxide becomes the gas in excess.

front:
**True or False?**

Oxygen is always a waste product in a plant.
back:
**False.**

Oxygen is a **waste product of photosynthesis** but a **reactant in respiration** — which gas is in excess depends on the time of day.

front: During the day, why is less carbon dioxide released than used?
back: Because **photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide faster** than respiration produces it, so there is a net **uptake** of carbon dioxide.

front: Define **excretion**.
back: The removal of the **waste substances of metabolic reactions**, **toxic materials**, and **substances in excess** of requirements.

front: Name the metabolic wastes produced by the human body.
back:
- **Carbon dioxide** and **water**, from aerobic respiration in cells
- **Urea**, from the breakdown of excess amino acids in the liver

front: Why is a build-up of carbon dioxide dangerous?
back: It dissolves easily in water to form an **acidic solution**, which **lowers the pH of cells** and can **reduce enzyme activity**.

front: What osmotic problem can a build-up of waste cause?
back: Body fluids become **more concentrated**, so **water moves out of the cells** by osmosis and essential reactions can no longer take place.

front: How does urea travel from the liver to the kidneys?
back: Dissolved in the **blood plasma**.

front: Name the three organs of excretion in humans.
back:
- **Kidneys**
- **Lungs**
- **Skin**

front: What do the kidneys excrete, and how?
back: **Urea**, **water** and **excess ions**, excreted in the **urine**.

front: What do the lungs excrete, and how?
back: **Carbon dioxide** and **water** as vapour, both leaving during **exhalation**.

front: What does the skin excrete, and how?
back: **Excess mineral ions** such as sodium, **water**, and some **urea** — all lost via **sweating**.

front: Where is urea produced?
back: In the **liver**, by the breakdown of **excess amino acids**.

front: The kidneys excrete urea, water and excess ions in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: The kidneys excrete urea, water and excess ions in the **urine**.

front: Excretion at the skin surface happens by ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Excretion at the skin surface happens by **sweating**.

front:
**True or False?**

Faeces is an example of excretion.
back:
**False.**

Faeces consists mainly of **undigested food**, not waste from metabolism, so it is **egestion**, not excretion.

front:
**True or False?**

Water is excreted by all three excretory organs.
back:
**True.**

The **kidneys** excrete it in urine, the **lungs** as vapour in exhaled air, and the **skin** in sweat.

front: Define **stimulus**.
back: A **change in the environment** that can be detected by an organism — for example light, temperature, sound, chemicals or touch.

front: Define **receptor**.
back:
A structure that **detects a stimulus**.

In humans, receptors are found in the **sense organs**.

front: Why must organisms respond to changes in their environment?
back: In order to **survive** — for example escaping predators, finding food, or maintaining internal conditions.

front: How do plants detect stimuli?
back: Using **specialised cells** that detect stimuli such as **light**, **gravity** or **water**.

front: Give three examples of a response to a stimulus.
back:
- **Moving** towards or away from something
- **Secreting chemicals**
- **Adjusting body processes**

front: Name five stimuli an organism might detect.
back:
- **Light**
- **Temperature**
- **Sound**
- **Chemicals**
- **Touch**

front: Where are receptors found in humans?
back: In the **sense organs**.

front: A change in the environment that an organism can detect is called a ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: A change in the environment that an organism can detect is called a **stimulus**.

front: Stimuli are detected by ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, which in humans are found in the sense organs.
back: Stimuli are detected by **receptors**, which in humans are found in the sense organs.

front:
**True or False?**

Only animals can detect and respond to stimuli.
back:
**False.**

Plants also detect stimuli, using **specialised cells** sensitive to light, gravity and water.

front:
**True or False?**

Responding to stimuli improves an organism's chance of survival.
back:
**True.**

It lets the organism escape predators, find food and keep its internal conditions within safe limits.

front: Put stimulus, receptor and response in the correct order.
back: **Stimulus ➔ receptor ➔ response**

front: Define **homeostasis**.
back: The **maintenance of a constant internal environment**.

front: Why is homeostasis essential?
back:
It keeps **optimal conditions** for **enzyme activity** and **cell function**, letting the organism survive and respond to change.

If conditions go beyond set limits, the organism may **die**.

front: Give two examples of homeostasis in humans.
back:
- Control of **body temperature**
- Control of **body water content**

front: What is the human core body temperature?
back: Close to **37 °C**.

front: Why must body temperature be kept close to 37 °C?
back: Because the body's **enzymes** work best at this temperature — much above it they **denature**, and much below it reactions become too slow.

front: How does the skin help to cool the body when it is too hot?
back:
- **Sweat** is released and **evaporates**, taking heat energy away from the body
- **Vasodilation** — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, so more heat is lost

front: By which three routes does the body lose water?
back:
- The **lungs**, in breathed-out air
- The **skin**, in sweat
- The **kidneys**, in urine

front: Define **internal environment**.
back: The conditions **inside the body** that surround the cells, such as **temperature** and **water content**.

front: What three things are needed for a co-ordinated response?
back:
- A **stimulus**
- A **receptor**
- An **effector**

front: What is the job of an **effector**?
back: It **carries out the response** — for example a **muscle** contracting or a **gland** releasing a hormone.

front: Give one example of an organism responding to a change in its environment.
back: A plant **shoot growing towards light**, or a person **shivering** when the air turns cold.

front: A ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ is a change in the environment that a receptor detects.
back: A **stimulus** is a change in the environment that a receptor detects.

front: When the body is too cold, blood vessels near the skin surface narrow — this is called ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: When the body is too cold, blood vessels near the skin surface narrow — this is called **vasoconstriction**.

front:
**True or False?**

Homeostasis is under conscious control.
back:
**False.**

Homeostasis is **involuntary** — you do not consciously maintain your body temperature or water content.

front:
**True or False?**

Homeostasis means the internal environment never changes at all.
back:
**False.**

Conditions **fluctuate slightly** around a set level — homeostasis keeps them **within narrow limits**, not perfectly fixed.

front: What three things does a co-ordinated response require?
back:
- A **stimulus** — a change in the environment
- A **receptor** — which detects the stimulus
- An **effector** — a muscle or gland that brings about the response

front: What is an effector?
back: A **muscle** or **gland** that brings about a response to **restore optimum levels**.

front: Which part of the body processes information from receptors?
back: The **central nervous system** — the **brain** and the **spinal cord**.

front: Why is homeostasis described as involuntary control?
back: Because it is **automatic** — the **brain** and **spinal cord** maintain it without any conscious thought.

front: Which two types of response can automatic control systems use?
back:
- **Nervous** responses
- **Chemical** responses, for example via **hormones**

front: Give two examples of a stimulus in a homeostatic response.
back:
- A change in **glucose levels** in the blood
- A change in **body temperature**

front: What does the central nervous system do in a response?
back: It **receives and processes information** from the receptors, then sends impulses out to the **effectors**.

front: An ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ is a muscle or gland that brings about a response.
back: An **effector** is a muscle or gland that brings about a response.

front: Impulses from receptors travel into the central nervous ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, made up of the brain and spinal cord.
back: Impulses from receptors travel into the central nervous **system**, made up of the brain and spinal cord.

front:
**True or False?**

All co-ordinated responses use the nervous system.
back:
**False.**

Some are **nervous** responses, but others are **chemical** responses carried by **hormones**.

front:
**True or False?**

A receptor and an effector do the same job.
back:
**False.**

A **receptor detects** the stimulus; an **effector** — a muscle or gland — **carries out** the response.

front: Put the parts of a co-ordinated response in order.
back: **Stimulus ➔ receptor ➔ effector ➔ response**

front: Define **tropism**.
back: A **directional growth response** made by a plant to a stimulus such as **light** or **gravity**.

front: What makes a tropism positive or negative?
back:
- **Positive** — growth **towards** the stimulus
- **Negative** — growth **away from** the stimulus

front: Why do plants need to respond to light and gravity?
back: To ensure their **leaves absorb light** for photosynthesis, and that **shoots grow upwards** while **roots grow downwards**.

front: Define **phototropism**.
back: Growth **towards or away from the direction of a light source**.

front: Define **geotropism**.
back: Growth **towards or away from the source of gravity**. Also called gravitropism.

front: Which tropisms do shoots show, and why?
back: **Positive phototropic** and **negative geotropic** — they grow **upwards, towards light**, so the leaves can absorb sunlight.

front: Which tropisms do roots show, and why?
back: **Negative phototropic** and **positive geotropic** — they grow **downwards into the soil**, to anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals.

front: Define **auxin**.
back: A **plant growth regulator**, similar to an animal hormone, that **co-ordinates and controls directional growth responses** such as phototropism.

front: Where is auxin made, and where does it act?
back: It is mostly made in the **tips of growing shoots**, then **diffuses down** to the region just below the tip where **cell division** occurs.

front: What effect does auxin have on cells?
back: It stimulates them to **elongate** — get longer. The **more auxin** present, the **faster** they elongate and grow.

front: Explain how a shoot bends towards a light source.
back:
When light shines **predominantly from one side**, auxin made in the tip concentrates on the **shaded side**.

Cells on the shaded side **elongate faster** than those on the sunny side.

This **unequal growth** makes the shoot **bend towards the light**.

front: What happens if light shines evenly all around a shoot tip?
back: Auxin is distributed **evenly**, so the cells grow at the **same rate** and the shoot grows straight up.

front: In a shoot lit from one side, auxin concentrates on the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ side.
back: In a shoot lit from one side, auxin concentrates on the **shaded** side.

front: Roots show a positive ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ response, growing downwards towards gravity.
back: Roots show a positive **geotropic** response, growing downwards towards gravity.

front:
**True or False?**

Auxin makes a shoot bend by increasing the number of cells.
back:
**False.**

Auxin causes the cells that **already exist** to **elongate**. It does not increase the overall number of cells.

front:
**True or False?**

Only the region behind the tip of a shoot contributes to growth.
back:
**True.**

Cell division and cell elongation happen **just below the tip**, which is where auxin diffuses to.

front: Name the two control systems that respond to stimuli in humans.
back:
- The **nervous system**
- The **hormonal system**, also called the **endocrine system**

front: How is information sent through the nervous system?
back: As **electrical impulses**, which pass very quickly along nerve cells called **neurones**.

front: How is information sent through the endocrine system?
back: As **chemical substances** called **hormones**, carried in the **blood** so they circulate round the whole body.

front: Define **gland**.
back: A group of cells that **produces and releases** one or more substances — a process known as **secretion**.

front: Which system controls functions needing an instant response?
back: The **nervous system** — for example the **withdrawal reflex** when a hand touches a flame.

front: What do hormones act on?
back: One or more specific **target organs**, whose activity they alter.

front: Compare what the nervous and endocrine systems are made of.
back:
- **Nervous system** — nerves (bundles of neurones), the brain and the spinal cord
- **Endocrine system** — **glands**

front: Compare the speed of the nervous and endocrine systems.
back:
- **Nervous** — **very fast**
- **Endocrine** — **slower**

front: Compare the type of effect each system has.
back:
- **Nervous** — **specific and localised**, acting on particular cells
- **Endocrine** — **widespread**, affecting many cells or organs

front: Compare how long the effects of each system last.
back:
- **Nervous** — **short**, stopping quickly
- **Endocrine** — **long**, lasting until the hormone is broken down

front: Hormones are transported around the body in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Hormones are transported around the body in the **blood**.

front: Electrical impulses pass along nerve cells called ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Electrical impulses pass along nerve cells called **neurones**.

front:
**True or False?**

Hormonal responses are faster than nervous responses.
back:
**False.**

Nervous responses are **very fast**; hormonal responses are **slower** but last longer.

front:
**True or False?**

A hormone can affect many organs at once.
back:
**True.**

Because hormones travel in the **blood** to the whole body, their effects are **widespread**.

front: What two structures make up the central nervous system?
back:
- The **brain**
- The **spinal cord**

front: What is the peripheral nervous system?
back: All of the **nerves** that branch out from the **CNS** to the rest of the body.

front: Define **nerve**.
back: A **bundle of neurones**.

front: How is information transmitted through the nervous system?
back: As **electrical impulses** — fast-moving electrical signals that pass along cells called **neurones**.

front: What is the role of the CNS?
back: It acts as the **central co-ordinating centre**, **processing incoming information** from the sense organs and **co-ordinating the body's response**.

front: What happens when a receptor is stimulated?
back: It produces **electrical impulses**, which travel along **sensory neurones** to the **CNS**.

front: Which neurones carry impulses away from the CNS?
back: **Motor neurones**, which carry impulses to the **effectors** — muscles or glands.

front: Give the full pathway of a nervous response.
back: **Stimulus ➔ receptor ➔ sensory neurone ➔ CNS ➔ motor neurone ➔ effector ➔ response**

front: What does an effector do?
back: It **carries out the response** — for example a **muscle contracts** or a **gland secretes**.

front: Name five stimuli that receptors in sense organs detect.
back:
- **Light**
- **Sound**
- **Touch**
- **Temperature**
- **Chemicals**

front: The central nervous system consists of the brain and the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: The central nervous system consists of the brain and the **spinal cord**.

front: Impulses travel to the CNS along ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ neurones.
back: Impulses travel to the CNS along **sensory** neurones.

front:
**True or False?**

A nerve and a neurone are the same thing.
back:
**False.**

A **neurone** is a single nerve cell. A **nerve** is a **bundle of neurones**.

front:
**True or False?**

Nerves link the CNS to the sense organs.
back:
**True.**

Nerves extend from the CNS to all areas of the body, including the sense organs, allowing communication between the brain and the rest of the body.

front: Define **synapse**.
back: The **tiny gap between two neurones**.

front: Define **neurotransmitter**.
back: A **chemical messenger** released at a synapse that carries the signal from one neurone to the next.

front: Describe how an impulse crosses a synapse.
back:
The electrical impulse reaches the end of one neurone and triggers the release of **neurotransmitters**.

These **diffuse across the synapse** and **bind to the next neurone**.

This causes a **new electrical impulse** to be generated.

front: Why are neurotransmitters needed at all?
back: Because neurones are **not directly connected** to each other — there is a gap, so the signal cannot pass electrically.

front: By which process do neurotransmitters cross the synapse?
back: **Diffusion**.

front: What triggers the release of neurotransmitters?
back: An **electrical impulse** arriving at the **end of a neurone**.

front: What happens after a neurotransmitter binds to the next neurone?
back: A **new electrical impulse** is generated, so the signal continues along the pathway.

front: The tiny gap between two neurones is called a ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: The tiny gap between two neurones is called a **synapse**.

front: Neurotransmitters cross the synapse by ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ and bind to the next neurone.
back: Neurotransmitters cross the synapse by **diffusion** and bind to the next neurone.

front:
**True or False?**

An electrical impulse jumps directly across a synapse.
back:
**False.**

The signal crosses **chemically**, carried by **neurotransmitters** that diffuse across the gap, before a new impulse is generated.

front:
**True or False?**

Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers.
back:
**True.**

They are released at the end of one neurone and bind to the next, passing the signal on.

front: Are neurones directly connected to one another?
back: **No.** They are separated by a **synapse**, a tiny gap.

front: Define **reflex response**.
back:
An **involuntary response** that does **not involve the conscious part of the brain** as the co-ordinator.

Awareness of it comes **after** the response has happened.

front: Define **reflex arc**.
back: The **pathway** taken by electrical impulses during a **reflex action**.

front: Why are reflex responses useful?
back: They are **automatic and rapid**, which helps **minimise damage** to the body and **aids survival**.

front: Give three examples of reflex responses.
back:
- **Pain withdrawal**
- **Blinking**
- **Coughing**

front: Describe the reflex arc for withdrawing a finger from a hot object.
back:
A **receptor** in the skin detects the **stimulus**.

A **sensory neurone** sends impulses to the **spinal cord**, which acts as the co-ordinator.

The impulse passes to a **relay neurone** in the spinal cord.

The relay neurone **synapses** with a **motor neurone**.

The motor neurone carries the impulse to a **muscle** (the **effector**), which **contracts** and pulls the finger away.

front: Which structure acts as the co-ordinator in a reflex arc?
back: The **spinal cord**, part of the **CNS** — not the conscious part of the brain.

front: Which neurone sits between the sensory and motor neurones?
back: The **relay neurone**, in the spinal cord.

front: What is the effector in a withdrawal reflex?
back: A **muscle**, which **contracts** to pull the body part away from the harmful stimulus.

front: Give the order of structures in a reflex arc.
back: **Stimulus ➔ receptor ➔ sensory neurone ➔ relay neurone ➔ motor neurone ➔ effector ➔ response**

front: In a reflex arc, the impulse passes to a ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ neurone in the spinal cord.
back: In a reflex arc, the impulse passes to a **relay** neurone in the spinal cord.

front: A reflex response is also known as an ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ response.
back: A reflex response is also known as an **involuntary** response.

front:
**True or False?**

You are aware of a reflex before it happens.
back:
**False.**

Awareness of a reflex comes **after** the response has already been carried out — which is what makes it so fast.

front:
**True or False?**

Blinking is a reflex response.
back:
**True.**

Like coughing and pain withdrawal, it is automatic and helps avoid serious injury — in this case damage to the eye.

front: Why is the eye described as a sense organ?
back: It is a highly specialised organ containing **receptor cells** that allow us to detect the stimulus of **light**.

front: What is the function of the conjunctiva?
back:
A **clear membrane** covering the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.

It **lubricates** the eye and **protects** it from external irritants.

front: What is the function of the cornea?
back: A **transparent, curved layer** at the front of the eye that **refracts light** as it enters.

front: What is the function of the sclera?
back: The **strong outer wall** of the eyeball. It **keeps the eye in shape** and provides attachment for the muscles that move the eye.

front: What is the function of the pupil?
back: A **circular opening** in the centre of the iris that **allows light to enter** the eye.

front: What is the function of the iris?
back: It **controls how much light enters the pupil**.

front: What is the function of the lens?
back: A **transparent disc** that can **change shape** to **focus light onto the retina**.

front: What is the function of the ciliary muscle?
back: A **ring of muscle** that **contracts and relaxes** to change the **shape of the lens**.

front: What is the function of the suspensory ligaments?
back: They **connect the ciliary muscle to the lens**.

front: What is the function of the retina?
back: It contains the **receptor cells sensitive to light**.

front: In which order does light pass through the eye?
back:
**Cornea ➔ pupil ➔ lens ➔ retina**

Impulses then leave the eye along the **optic nerve**.

front: What is the function of the optic nerve?
back: It **carries impulses between the eye and the brain**.

front: What is the blind spot?
back: The point where the **optic nerve leaves the eye**, at which there are **no light receptor cells**.

front: Light-sensitive receptor cells are found in the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ of the eye.
back: Light-sensitive receptor cells are found in the **retina** of the eye.

front: Light is refracted as it enters the eye by the transparent, curved ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Light is refracted as it enters the eye by the transparent, curved **cornea**.

front:
**True or False?**

The suspensory ligaments are muscles.
back:
**False.**

They are **ligaments** connecting the ciliary muscle to the lens — they **tighten or loosen**, they do not contract.

front:
**True or False?**

There are no light receptor cells at the blind spot.
back:
**True.**

It is the point where the **optic nerve leaves the eye**.

front: Define **accommodation**.
back: The way the **lens** brings about the **fine focusing** of light onto the retina.

front: How is the shape of the lens changed?
back: The lens is **elastic**. The **ciliary muscles** contract or relax, which makes the **suspensory ligaments** tighten or loosen and so changes the lens shape.

front: Describe how the eye focuses on a close-up object.
back:
The **ciliary muscles contract**, so the ring of muscle decreases in diameter.

The **suspensory ligaments loosen**, so they stop pulling on the lens.

The lens becomes **thicker**, and light is refracted **more**.

front: Describe how the eye focuses on a distant object.
back:
The **ciliary muscles relax**, so the ring of muscle increases in diameter.

The **suspensory ligaments tighten** and pull on the lens.

The lens becomes **thinner**, and light is refracted **less**.

front: What is the purpose of the pupil reflex?
back: To **protect the retina from damage** by controlling how much light enters the eye.

front: What happens to the pupil in dim light, and why?
back: It **dilates** (widens), to let **as much light as possible** into the eye and improve vision.

front: What happens to the pupil in bright light, and why?
back: It **constricts** (narrows), to stop **too much light** entering and **damaging the retina**.

front: Why can you not see clearly for a moment in bright sunlight?
back:
The **pupil** takes a moment to **constrict**.

Until it does, **too much light** reaches the retina.

front: Which part of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
back: The **iris**, a ring of muscle surrounding the pupil.

front: To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes **thicker**.

front: In bright light the pupil ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ to protect the retina from damage.
back: In bright light the pupil **constricts** to protect the retina from damage.

front:
**True or False?**

The suspensory ligaments contract to change the lens shape.
back:
**False.**

Suspensory ligaments are **not muscles** — they **tighten or loosen**. It is the **ciliary muscles** that contract and relax.

front:
**True or False?**

The pupil reflex is an example of a reflex action.
back:
**True.**

It happens automatically, without conscious thought, to protect the retina.

front: Which lens shape refracts light more, and when is it used?
back: A **thicker (fatter)** lens refracts light **more**, and is used when focusing on **near objects**.

front: Why is the skin described as our largest sense organ?
back: It contains many **receptors** that detect external stimuli, including **touch, pressure, pain, heat and cold**.

front: Define **vasodilation**.
back: When the muscles in the walls of the **arterioles** near the skin **relax**, so the arterioles **widen** and **more blood** flows through the skin capillaries.

front: Define **vasoconstriction**.
back: When the muscles in the walls of the **arterioles** near the skin **contract**, so the arterioles **narrow** and **less blood** flows through the skin capillaries.

front: How does vasodilation cool the body?
back: A **greater volume of blood** flows through the capillaries near the skin surface, so more heat is **lost to the environment by radiation**.

front: How does vasoconstriction reduce heat loss?
back: A **smaller volume of blood** reaches the skin capillaries, so **less heat is lost by radiation**.

front: How does sweating cool the body?
back: Sweat is secreted by the **sweat glands** and **evaporates**, using **heat energy from the body** to convert liquid water into water vapour.

front: Describe how the skin responds when a person enters a hot room.
back:
**Vasodilation** — arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen, so more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost by **radiation**.

**Sweating** — sweat evaporates from the skin surface, cooling the body.

front: Describe how the skin responds in a cold environment.
back:
**Vasoconstriction** — arterioles supplying the skin capillaries narrow, reducing blood flow to the skin and so reducing heat loss.

**Sweating decreases** — less sweat is produced, so less heat is lost by evaporation.

front: Why is vasoconstriction not strictly a warming mechanism?
back: It does **not raise the temperature of the blood** — it only **reduces heat loss** from blood flowing through the skin.

front: Why does sweating stop cooling you on a very humid day?
back:
Sweat only cools the body when it **evaporates**.

In humid air the water vapour cannot escape easily, so evaporation slows and less heat is removed.

front: Where are the receptors that detect a change in temperature?
back: In the **skin**, which contains both **heat receptors** and **cold receptors**.

front: Why must core body temperature be tightly controlled?
back: Because the body's **enzymes** work best close to **37 °C** — far above it they **denature**, and far below it reactions become too slow.

front: During ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ the arterioles near the skin widen so more heat is lost by radiation.
back: During **vasodilation** the arterioles near the skin widen so more heat is lost by radiation.

front: Sweat cools the skin as it ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿, using heat energy from the body.
back: Sweat cools the skin as it **evaporates**, using heat energy from the body.

front:
**True or False?**

Vasodilation means the capillaries in the skin get wider.
back:
**False.**

It is the **arterioles** that widen. That lets **more blood** flow through the skin capillaries.

front:
**True or False?**

Heat exchange happens at the body's surface.
back:
**True.**

The surface is where the blood comes into **closest proximity to the environment**, so it is where heat is both lost and gained.

front: Define **hormone**.
back: A **chemical substance** produced by a **gland** and **carried by the blood**, which **alters the activity** of one or more specific **target organs**.

front: Where is adrenaline produced, and what is its role?
back:
In the **adrenal gland**.

It readies the body for a **'fight or flight'** response, in situations where the body may be in danger.

front: Give four effects of adrenaline.
back:
- **Increased heart and breathing rate**, delivering glucose and oxygen faster
- **Blood flow redirected to the muscles**, away from non-essential organs
- **Dilation of blood vessels in the muscles**
- **Breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose** in the liver and muscle cells

front: Where is insulin produced, and what is its role?
back:
In the **pancreas**, which acts as an **endocrine gland**.

Its role is to **lower blood glucose levels**.

front: Describe what happens when blood glucose gets too high.
back:
Cells in the **pancreas** detect the rise and secrete **insulin** into the blood.

Insulin stimulates the **muscles and liver** to **take up glucose** and store it as **glycogen**.

Blood glucose falls back to normal, and the pancreas stops secreting insulin.

front: Why is a blood glucose level that is too high dangerous?
back: Cells of the body can **lose water by osmosis**.

front: Why is a blood glucose level that is too low dangerous?
back: The **brain receives insufficient glucose** for respiration, which can lead to a **coma** or even **death**.

front: Where is testosterone produced, and what is its role?
back:
In the male **testes**.

It stimulates the development of the **male reproductive organs** and the **secondary sexual characteristics in males** — facial, pubic and underarm hair, deepening of the voice, and increased muscle mass.

front: Where is progesterone produced, and what is its role?
back:
In the female **ovaries**.

It **maintains the uterine lining** during pregnancy and **prevents further ovulation**.

front: Where is oestrogen produced, and what is its role?
back:
In the female **ovaries**.

It causes the **secondary sexual characteristics in females** — breast development, wider hips, pubic and underarm hair — and helps **regulate the menstrual cycle**.

front: How does oestrogen help regulate the menstrual cycle?
back: It stimulates the **repair and thickening of the uterus lining** after menstruation, preparing it to receive a fertilised egg.

front: Which two organs work together to control blood glucose levels?
back:
- The **pancreas**
- The **liver**

front: Insulin causes excess blood glucose to be stored in the liver and muscles as ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Insulin causes excess blood glucose to be stored in the liver and muscles as **glycogen**.

front: Adrenaline is produced by the ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ gland.
back: Adrenaline is produced by the **adrenal** gland.

front:
**True or False?**

The pancreas only produces hormones.
back:
**False.**

It acts as an **endocrine gland**, secreting insulin into the blood, but it also has a separate **digestive** role, secreting **enzymes** into the digestive system.

front:
**True or False?**

Control of blood glucose is an example of homeostasis.
back:
**True.**

Blood glucose concentration must be kept within a **narrow range**, just like core body temperature.

front: What does the acronym **MRS C GREN** stand for?
back:
The eight life processes shared by all living organisms:

- **M**ovement
- **R**espiration
- **S**ensitivity
- **C**ontrol
- **G**rowth
- **R**eproduction
- **E**xcretion
- **N**utrition

front:
**True or False?**

Reproduction is the only life process that viruses appear to carry out.
back:
**True.**

Viruses are not considered living because they do not carry out all eight life processes for themselves. Even to reproduce, they must **take over a host cell's metabolic pathways**.

front: How does nutrition in plants differ from nutrition in animals?
back:
Plants **make their own food** by photosynthesis, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.

Animals **consume other living organisms** and break the large molecules down by **digestion** into simpler molecules they can absorb.

front: Define **respiration**.
back: A chemical process carried out in **all living organisms** in which **energy is released from glucose**, either in the presence of oxygen (aerobic) or in its absence (anaerobic).

front: Respiration releases energy from glucose and transfers it in the form of ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Respiration releases energy from glucose and transfers it in the form of **ATP**.

front: Define **excretion**.
back: The **removal of toxic materials** and the waste products of **metabolic reactions** from an organism.

front: How does excretion differ from egestion?
back:
**Excretion** removes waste that has come from **chemical reactions inside cells**, such as carbon dioxide, water and urea.

**Egestion** removes **faeces** — the remains of food that was never absorbed during digestion.

front: Urea is a nitrogen-containing waste product formed in animals from the breakdown of ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Urea is a nitrogen-containing waste product formed in animals from the breakdown of **proteins**.

front: Define **sensitivity**.
back: The ability of an organism to **detect and respond to stimuli** in its surroundings.

front: What is the difference between geotropism and phototropism?
back:
**Geotropism** is a plant's growth response to **gravity**, which makes roots grow down into the soil.

**Phototropism** is a plant's growth response to **light**, which makes shoots grow towards sunlight.

front: Define **locomotion**.
back: The movement of an organism **from one place to another**.

front:
**True or False?**

Plants show no movement at all.
back:
**False.**

Plants cannot move from place to place, but they can **change their orientation** — for example, sunflowers track the sun through the day.

front: Define **homeostasis**.
back: The **control of an organism's internal conditions** so that they are kept within required limits.

front: Name two ways the human body responds to a rise in body temperature.
back:
- **Sweating**
- **Vasodilation**

Both return the body to its optimum temperature of **37 °C**.

front: Which waste products do plants excrete?
back:
- **Oxygen**, a waste product of photosynthesis
- **Carbon dioxide**, a waste product of respiration

Both are lost through the **stomata** of the leaf.

front: How does sexual reproduction differ from asexual reproduction?
back:
In **sexual** reproduction, male and female **gametes fuse**, so the offspring's DNA comes from **both parents**.

In **asexual** reproduction there is only **one parent**, so the offspring is a **clone** with DNA identical to the parent's.

front: Define **growth**.
back:
A **permanent increase in size**.

Animals grow between the zygote and adult stage, with changes in shape and proportion. Plants keep growing **throughout their whole life**, forming new shoots, leaves and branches year after year.

front: Define **eukaryotic organism**.
back:
An organism whose cells contain a **nucleus** surrounded by a **distinct membrane**.

Eukaryotes may be **multicellular or single-celled**.

front: Name the four groups of eukaryotic organisms.
back:
- **Animals**
- **Plants**
- **Fungi**
- **Protoctists**

front: All eukaryotic cells contain a ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ surrounded by a distinct membrane.
back: All eukaryotic cells contain a **nucleus** surrounded by a distinct membrane.

front: Give two ways a prokaryotic cell differs from a eukaryotic cell.
back:
- Prokaryotes have **no nucleus** — their genetic material sits in the **cytoplasm** as a single circular chromosome of DNA
- Prokaryotes are **always single-celled**, and their cells are substantially **smaller**

front: State three features of animal cells.
back:
- **Multicellular**, with a nucleus in a distinct membrane
- **No cellulose cell walls** and **no chloroplasts**, so they cannot photosynthesise
- Carbohydrate is often stored as **glycogen**

front: Which two features of animals are linked to finding food and escaping danger?
back:
- **Nervous coordination**
- The ability to **move from place to place**

front: What are plant cell walls made of?
back: **Cellulose**.

front: As which carbohydrates do plants store their food?
back:
**Starch** or **sucrose**.

This contrasts with animals and fungi, which store carbohydrate as **glycogen**.

front:
**True or False?**

All fungi are multicellular.
back:
**False.**

Most fungi are multicellular, such as *Mucor*, but some are **single-celled** — for example, **yeast**.

front: Define **hyphae**.
back: The **thread-like structures** that make up the body of a multicellular fungus. Each one contains **many nuclei**.

front: Define **mycelium**.
back: The **network of hyphae** that forms the body of a multicellular fungus.

front: Define **saprotrophic nutrition**.
back: Feeding by **secreting digestive enzymes outside the body** onto food, usually decaying organic matter, and then **absorbing the digested products**.

front: What are fungal cell walls made of?
back: **Chitin**.

front: Why are protoctists described as a very diverse group?
back:
Because they have features unlike the other three eukaryotic groups, and unlike each other:

- Some are **animal-like**, such as *Amoeba* and *Plasmodium*
- Some are **plant-like**, with **cell walls and chloroplasts**, such as the green alga *Chlorella*

front: Are protoctists single-celled or multicellular?
back: **Microscopic and single-celled**.

front: The protoctist ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ is a pathogen that causes malaria in humans.
back: The protoctist ***Plasmodium*** is a pathogen that causes malaria in humans.

front:
**True or False?**

Plants, fungi and protoctists all lack nervous coordination.
back:
**True.**

Of the four eukaryotic groups, only **animals** usually have nervous coordination.

front: Define **prokaryotic organism**.
back:
A **single-celled** organism whose cell has **no nucleus**, with its nuclear material found in the **cytoplasm**.

**Bacteria** are prokaryotic organisms.

front: State three features shown by all prokaryotic organisms.
back:
- They are **single-celled**
- They have **no nucleus**
- Their **nuclear material** is found in the **cytoplasm**

front: Which four structures are found in a bacterial cell?
back:
- **Cell wall**
- **Cell membrane**
- **Cytoplasm**
- **Plasmids**

front: Bacteria lack a nucleus but contain a circular chromosome of ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Bacteria lack a nucleus but contain a circular chromosome of **DNA**.

front:
**True or False?**

Bacterial cells contain mitochondria.
back:
**False.**

Bacteria **lack mitochondria** and have **no other membrane-bound organelles**.

front: How are bacteria described in terms of size and cell number?
back: They are **microscopic, single-celled organisms**.

front: Name the rod-shaped bacterium used to make yoghurt from milk.
back: ***Lactobacillus bulgaricus***.

front: Name the spherical bacterium that causes pneumonia.
back: ***Pneumococcus***.

front: How do most bacteria feed?
back:
On **other living or dead organisms**.

Only **some** bacteria can photosynthesise and make their own food.

front:
**True or False?**

No bacteria are able to photosynthesise.
back:
**False.**

**Some** bacteria can photosynthesise, although **most** feed off other living or dead organisms.

front: Define **plasmid**.
back: A **small circular loop of DNA** in a bacterial cell, separate from its main circular chromosome.

front: Where is the genetic material found in prokaryotes and in eukaryotes?
back:
- **Prokaryotes** — in the **cytoplasm**
- **Eukaryotes** — in a **nucleus**

front: Do all prokaryotic cells have a cell wall?
back:
**Yes** — all prokaryotes have a cell wall.

Only **some** eukaryotes do, such as plants and fungi.

front: ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿ are prokaryotic organisms, so their cells have no nucleus.
back: **Bacteria** are prokaryotic organisms, so their cells have no nucleus.

front: Define **pathogen**.
back: An organism that **causes disease** in another organism.

front: Name the four groups of organisms that include pathogens.
back:
- **Bacteria**
- **Fungi**
- **Protoctists**
- **Viruses**

front: Describe the shapes and sizes of viruses.
back: They have a **wide variety of shapes and sizes**, and are **always smaller than bacteria**.

front: Name the disease each of the three named viruses causes.
back:
- **Tobacco mosaic virus** — discolouring of the leaves of tobacco plants
- **Influenza virus** — flu
- **HIV** — AIDS

front:
**True or False?**

All pathogens are bacteria.
back:
**False.**

Pathogens may also be **fungi**, **protoctists** or **viruses**.

front: Which organism causes severe malaria in humans?
back: The protoctist ***Plasmodium falciparum***.

front: Viruses are small particles that are always smaller than ＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿.
back: Viruses are small particles that are always smaller than **bacteria**.

front:
**True or False?**

Viruses are classified as living organisms.
back:
**False.**
